title: the mountain of herbs
hook: how one flight became the picture on a million walls

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mountain of herbs. Its scent lifted the fallen army, and Hanuman carried the peak home. Did you give back something you borrowed? Today, how this story lives on outside the book, and the week closes. Day six hundred fifty-one.

Walk into a roadside shrine in North India, or a truck stop, or a grandmother's prayer room, and there's a good chance you'll see him: Hanuman in flight, mace in one hand, a mountain balanced on the other. Ask someone what's happening in the picture, and they'll probably tell you a slightly different story from the one we've just heard. Lakshmana is dying. There's a physician. There's a deadline at dawn. That version is real too. Here's where it comes from.
screen: `A PICTURE ON A MILLION WALLS.` → `LAKSHMANA IS DYING.` → `A DEADLINE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Valmiki actually tells a herb flight twice. The first is the one we've followed: after Indrajit's Brahma weapon, the whole army down, Jambavan sending Hanuman north. The second comes later, near the very end of the war, when Lakshmana alone is struck by a spear, and Sushena, the monkey physician, sends Hanuman for the herbs again. Over centuries, the two stories have flowed together in people's memories into one: Lakshmana wounded, the physician, the flight, the mountain, the race against the dawn. Later poets shaped that memory too. The Hanuman Chalisa, the forty-verse hymn many Hindus recite, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, says it in one line: he brought the life-giving herb, and Lakshmana lived, and Rama embraced him with joy. That's the line many people know, even if they've never opened Valmiki. So which is right? Both are part of the tradition. Valmiki is the oldest telling, and it keeps the two rescues apart. The later devotional tradition keeps the heart of it: Hanuman as the one who brings healing, against the clock, when everyone else is helpless. That's why so many people pray to him when someone they love is in hospital. And this closes a week that ran from a giant woken with drums, through a brother who fought for a brother he knew was wrong, to Lakshmana's great victory and great fall, an old bear's question in the dark, and a mountain flying south.
screen: `VALMIKI TELLS IT TWICE.` · `TWO RESCUES BECOME ONE.` · `THE HANUMAN CHALISA'S LINE.` · `THE ONE WHO BRINGS HEALING.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM DRUMS TO A FLYING MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone you know who is ill or struggling right now. Picture them gently. You don't need to fix anything. If you pray, you might hold them in prayer in your own way; if you don't, simply wish them ease. Breathe in, as if breathing in the scent of healing herbs. Breathe out toward them. The bell holds the time.
The mountain of herbs. In Valmiki, two healing flights; in the memory of millions, one picture: Hanuman with a mountain in his hand, bringing life back to Lakshmana.
Your line: the mountain of herbs. Today, send one message of care to someone who is unwell. Day six hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and images of Hanuman carrying the mountain hang in homes, temples and shops; people pray to him for the recovery of the sick.

fork.setup: you're a storyteller with one evening to tell the herb story. Valmiki has two flights. what do you do?
options: tell both, exactly as Valmiki has them.
tell one, with Lakshmana at the center.
fork.reveal: over centuries, many tellers did exactly that, which is why the picture most people know is Lakshmana, the physician and the dawn deadline.

original.note: Avadhi, from the Hanuman Chalisa: bringing the life-giving herb, you revived Lakhan (Lakshmana).

trapdoor: what you thought: there's one herb story, and Lakshmana is at its center.
what it means: Valmiki tells two herb flights, and the tradition has folded them into one beloved picture.
what a scholar hears: the Hanuman Chalisa, traditionally attributed to Tulsidas, carries the Lakshmana version in a single line.
